Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No

playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

- Provide light and dark appearance as intentional art direction, not simple color inversion.
- Include haptic feedback for meaningful interactions (at least card movement success/failure and win).
- Provide local stats for games played, games won, best time, and streak.
- Provide settings for draw count (1 vs 3), card back selection, timer on/off.
- Persist all user and game state locally and deterministically.
- Use a shared SwiftUI theme system for typography, spacing, colors, elevation, and motion.
- Respect accessibility and platform conventions (readability, contrast, hit testing, reduced-motion behavior where relevant).
- Use a clear visual hook that differentiates the app at a glance and is reusable across all states.
- No placeholder flows or screens in shipping experience.

Non-goals:
- No online features, social shares, friend leaderboards, remote sync, or multi-device persistence.
- No account management, no ad monetization, no in-app purchase system.
- No multi-game/multi-deck variants; not FreeCell/Spider/tri-peaks.
- No tutorial-first scaffolding that replaces playable game depth with setup instructions.
- No generic deck UI with placeholder card glyphs or flat placeholders.

Output shape:
- One iOS app deliverable (single user-facing product), with dedicated Game, Stats, and Settings surfaces and a coherent shell/nav pattern that does not dilute the game.
- Deterministic, local domain model for cards and game state.
- Visual system centralized in a theme layer that all views consume.
- Persisted state store plus separate UI state for in-flight interactions and animations.

Production-readiness definition:
- The app launches to a fully playable game screen, never a blank/wizard/placeholder shell.
- Core loop (play/move/undo/new game) functions without hidden assumptions.
- All promised settings and metrics are functional, persisted, and survivable across launch/relaunch.
- Both light and dark modes render complete, readable, intentional visuals.
- One screenshot in each appearance clearly reads as a premium native game, not a template.
- Verified locally that no network/framework calls can escape-device data flow.
- No known blockers in core gameplay logic and no contradictory placeholders in required screens.

- Any conflict between visual flourish and rule correctness is resolved in favor of correctness, input fidelity, and deterministic local state.
- Any requirement linked to legal move logic, state persistence, and undo integrity has priority over animation polish.
- If a card art/motion change affects discoverability or move accuracy, keep visual intent but simplify motion.
- If performance degrades under heavy rendering, remove non-critical effects before reducing gameplay responsiveness.
- If a requirement in this contract is not implemented and testable, it is out of scope and must be declared blocked.
- If architecture choice makes rule validation harder, choose simpler state modeling over “clever” architecture.
- A visual treatment is only accepted if it is consistent with and readable under both appearances.
- If a promise from the prompt is ambiguous, use the explicit assumptions below and freeze them until explicitly changed.

Assumptions to lock ambiguity:
- Klondike refers to single-deck standard layout with seven tableau columns and one foundation set per suit.
- Foundation movement is ascending with same-suit requirement; tableau movement is alternating colors and descending ranks.
- Waste-to-foundation/tableau rules follow standard legal sequence with only movable revealed cards and King-only empty tableau placement.
- Stock cycling behavior is fixed by settings semantics and must be documented in game help (no implicit unlimited reshuffle unless explicitly set).
- Timer starts on first action of a game and pauses when app is backgrounded, unless user disables timing in settings.

Numbered testable requirements:
1. User can start the app and play a complete game without any sign-in, account, or network dependency.
2. Creating a new game initializes a legal Klondike deal with all 52 cards in valid positions.
3. Stock, waste, four foundations, and seven tableau columns are always visible and consistent with Klondike structure.
4. Drag-and-drop or tap-to-move moves at least one legal move type without crash on first interaction.
5. The system blocks illegal moves and does not apply invalid state transitions.
6. A legal move updates source/destination piles exactly according to Klondike rules.
7. Win detection triggers only when all tableau and waste are empty and all foundations are complete.
8. Undo reverses the last committed move statefully, including source/destination and reveal state.
9. New game clears current progress and starts from a fresh deterministic local deal.
10. Draw-1 and draw-3 behavior follows the selected setting and changes gameplay immediately after start of next hand.
11. Settings changes persist across app relaunches.
12. Game stats (played, won, best time, streak) persist locally and update only from real sessions.
13. Streak increments only on user-validated victories and resets correctly on loss/abandon/new session flow.
14. Haptic feedback triggers on accepted moves, invalid move attempts (if any), and game win.
15. Cards render with custom face/back design, with the same visual grammar across suits/ranks and no SF Symbols as primary suit glyph style.
16. Card visuals and motion remain readable and performant in both light and dark modes.
17. Touching/dragging cards feels physically responsive with spring-influenced motion and no jitter at standard device fps.
18. Local state and settings are recoverable after app relaunch and do not leak to disk beyond app container.

- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

Original prompt (verbatim, preserved):

Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

I will treat this as a strict contract, not a suggestion list. The one thing this project stands for is “playable first, art second, but both at production quality.” The biggest risk in my own direction is overfitting to a unique visual style and accidentally creating a game that feels pretty but violates clarity or rules correctness, so I am setting correctness and touch responsiveness as hard gates for every phase.

Hard requirements:
- Native iOS app in SwiftUI (iOS 17+ target), no third-party dependencies unless absolutely necessary for stability or rendering that cannot be achieved natively.
- Purely local app behavior: no network, no backend, no sign-in, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash-reporting calls that leave device.
- Implement fully playable Klondike solitaire with legal move validation, win condition, undo, reset/new-game/deal, and complete stock/waste/foundation/tableau behavior.
- Support touch interactions that feel production-grade: either drag/drop or tap-to-move, both optional only if one is sufficient; at least one primary interaction must be flawless and accessible.
- Build a custom card system with unique visual identity on all 52 fronts plus back, including custom rank/suit treatments not derived from stock SF Symbols and a shared pattern grammar.
- Deliver tactile motion language: spring drag, believable flip/deal animation, and lightweight depth/parallax cues without harming frame rate or input response.
- Provide light and dark appearance as intentional art direction, not simple color inversion.
- Include haptic feedback for meaningful interactions (at least card movement success/failure and win).
- Provide local stats for games played, games won, best time, and streak.
- Provide settings for draw count (1 vs 3), card back selection, timer on/off.
- Persist all user and game state locally and deterministically.
- Use a shared SwiftUI theme system for typography, spacing, colors, elevation, and motion.
- Respect accessibility and platform conventions (readability, contrast, hit testing, reduced-motion behavior where relevant).
- Use a clear visual hook that differentiates the app at a glance and is reusable across all states.
- No placeholder flows or screens in shipping experience.

Non-goals:
- No online features, social shares, friend leaderboards, remote sync, or multi-device persistence.
- No account management, no ad monetization, no in-app purchase system.
- No multi-game/multi-deck variants; not FreeCell/Spider/tri-peaks.
- No tutorial-first scaffolding that replaces playable game depth with setup instructions.
- No generic deck UI with placeholder card glyphs or flat placeholders.

Output shape:
- One iOS app deliverable (single user-facing product), with dedicated Game, Stats, and Settings surfaces and a coherent shell/nav pattern that does not dilute the game.
- Deterministic, local domain model for cards and game state.
- Visual system centralized in a theme layer that all views consume.
- Persisted state store plus separate UI state for in-flight interactions and animations.

Production-readiness definition:
- The app launches to a fully playable game screen, never a blank/wizard/placeholder shell.
- Core loop (play/move/undo/new game) functions without hidden assumptions.
- All promised settings and metrics are functional, persisted, and survivable across launch/relaunch.
- Both light and dark modes render complete, readable, intentional visuals.
- One screenshot in each appearance clearly reads as a premium native game, not a template.
- Verified locally that no network/framework calls can escape-device data flow.
- No known blockers in core gameplay logic and no contradictory placeholders in required screens.

Decision rules for later phases:
- Any conflict between visual flourish and rule correctness is resolved in favor of correctness, input fidelity, and deterministic local state.
- Any requirement linked to legal move logic, state persistence, and undo integrity has priority over animation polish.
- If a card art/motion change affects discoverability or move accuracy, keep visual intent but simplify motion.
- If performance degrades under heavy rendering, remove non-critical effects before reducing gameplay responsiveness.
- If a requirement in this contract is not implemented and testable, it is out of scope and must be declared blocked.
- If architecture choice makes rule validation harder, choose simpler state modeling over “clever” architecture.
- A visual treatment is only accepted if it is consistent with and readable under both appearances.
- If a promise from the prompt is ambiguous, use the explicit assumptions below and freeze them until explicitly changed.

Assumptions to lock ambiguity:
- Klondike refers to single-deck standard layout with seven tableau columns and one foundation set per suit.
- Foundation movement is ascending with same-suit requirement; tableau movement is alternating colors and descending ranks.
- Waste-to-foundation/tableau rules follow standard legal sequence with only movable revealed cards and King-only empty tableau placement.
- Stock cycling behavior is fixed by settings semantics and must be documented in game help (no implicit unlimited reshuffle unless explicitly set).
- Timer starts on first action of a game and pauses when app is backgrounded, unless user disables timing in settings.

Numbered testable requirements:
1. User can start the app and play a complete game without any sign-in, account, or network dependency.
2. Creating a new game initializes a legal Klondike deal with all 52 cards in valid positions.
3. Stock, waste, four foundations, and seven tableau columns are always visible and consistent with Klondike structure.
4. Drag-and-drop or tap-to-move moves at least one legal move type without crash on first interaction.
5. The system blocks illegal moves and does not apply invalid state transitions.
6. A legal move updates source/destination piles exactly according to Klondike rules.
7. Win detection triggers only when all tableau and waste are empty and all foundations are complete.
8. Undo reverses the last committed move statefully, including source/destination and reveal state.
9. New game clears current progress and starts from a fresh deterministic local deal.
10. Draw-1 and draw-3 behavior follows the selected setting and changes gameplay immediately after start of next hand.
11. Settings changes persist across app relaunches.
12. Game stats (played, won, best time, streak) persist locally and update only from real sessions.
13. Streak increments only on user-validated victories and resets correctly on loss/abandon/new session flow.
14. Haptic feedback triggers on accepted moves, invalid move attempts (if any), and game win.
15. Cards render with custom face/back design, with the same visual grammar across suits/ranks and no SF Symbols as primary suit glyph style.
16. Card visuals and motion remain readable and performant in both light and dark modes.
17. Touching/dragging cards feels physically responsive with spring-influenced motion and no jitter at standard device fps.
18. Local state and settings are recoverable after app relaunch and do not leak to disk beyond app container.
